1. The Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle

Statement of the Problem

Consider the optimal control problem with an initial value: egin{align} \dot{x}(t) &= f(x(t), u(t))
x(0) &= x_0 \end{align}

The objective is to optimize the general cost function: \(J(u) = \Phi(x(T)) + \int_0^T L(x(t), u(t)) dt\)

Define the Hamiltonian function: egin{equation} H(x, u, p) = p^T \cdot f(x, u) + L(x, u) \end{equation}

Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle (PMP) yields the following relations: egin{align} \dot{x}^*(t) &= rac{\partial H}{\partial p}
\dot{p}(t) &= - rac{\partial H}{\partial x}
rac{\partial H}{\partial u} &= 0 \end{align}

Proof

Reference: Lawrence C. Evans, UC Berkeley, “An Introduction to Mathematical Optimal Control Theory”, Appendix.

a. Adjoint Equation

We prove (2), the adjoint equation: $\dot{p}(t) = - rac{\partial H}{\partial x}$.

Problem: First, consider the optimization problem with only the running cost: \(J = \int_0^T L(x, u) dt\) with the dynamic constraint: $f(x, u) - \dot{x}(t) = 0$.

Consider the Augmented Functional: \(\mathcal{L} = \int_0^T \left[ L(x, u) + p(t)^T (f(x, u) - \dot{x}) ight] dt\) Substituting the Hamiltonian function definition, we get: \(\mathcal{L} = \int_0^T \left( H(x, u, p) - p(t)^T \cdot \dot{x} ight) dt\)

Taking the first-order variation of $\mathcal{L}$: egin{equation} \Rightarrow \delta \mathcal{L} = \int_0^T \left[ rac{\partial H}{\partial x} \cdot \delta x - p(t)^T \cdot \delta \dot{x} ight] dt = 0 \label{eq:i} \end{equation} egin{equation} \Rightarrow \delta \mathcal{L} = \int_0^T \left( rac{\partial H}{\partial x} + \dot{p}(t)^T ight) \delta x \, dt = 0 \label{eq:ii} \end{equation} Since the integral is zero for all $\delta x$, the expression inside the integral must be zero: \( rac{\partial H}{\partial x} + \dot{p}^T = 0 \implies \dot{p}^T(t) = - rac{\partial H}{\partial x}\)

Proof of \eqref{eq:i}:

We introduce a perturbation to the state variable with parameter $\epsilon$: egin{align} ext{State: } & x(t, \epsilon) = x^(t) + \epsilon \cdot \eta(t) \implies \delta x = \epsilon \eta(t) onumber
ext{Velocity: } & \dot{x}(t, \epsilon) = \dot{x}^(t) + \epsilon \cdot \dot{\eta}(t) \implies \delta \dot{x} = \epsilon \dot{\eta}(t) onumber \end{align}

Consider the functional with respect to $\epsilon$: \(\mathcal{L}(\epsilon) = \int_0^T \left[ H(x(t, \epsilon), u, p) - p^T \cdot \dot{x}(t, \epsilon) ight] dt\)

Examine the derivative with respect to $\epsilon$: \( rac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\epsilon} = \int_0^T rac{\partial}{\partial \epsilon} \left[ H(x(t, \epsilon), u, p) - p^T \cdot \dot{x}(t, \epsilon) ight] dt\)

Applying the Chain Rule:

  • For the first component: \( rac{\partial H}{\partial \epsilon} = rac{\partial H}{\partial x} \cdot rac{\partial x}{\partial \epsilon}\) Since $x = x^*(t) + \epsilon \eta(t) \implies rac{\partial x}{\partial \epsilon} = \eta(t)$ Thus: \( rac{\partial H}{\partial \epsilon} = rac{\partial H}{\partial x} \cdot \eta(t)\)
  • For the second component: \( rac{\partial}{\partial \epsilon} \left( p^T \cdot \dot{x}(t, \epsilon) ight) = p^T \cdot \left( rac{\partial \dot{x}}{\partial \epsilon} ight)\) Since $\dot{x} = \dot{x}^* + \epsilon \cdot \dot{\eta}(t) \implies rac{\partial \dot{x}}{\partial \epsilon} = \dot{\eta}(t)$ Thus we get $p^T \cdot \dot{\eta}(t)$

Substituting into the integral: \( rac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\epsilon} = \int_0^T \left( rac{\partial H}{\partial x} \cdot \eta(t) - p^T \cdot \dot{\eta}(t) ight) dt\)

By definition of the first variation: $\delta \mathcal{L} = \left( rac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\epsilon} \Big|_{\epsilon=0} ight) \cdot \epsilon$. Multiplying the expression by $\epsilon$: egin{align} \delta \mathcal{L} &= \int_0^T \left[ rac{\partial H}{\partial x} (\epsilon \eta(t)) - p^T (\epsilon \dot{\eta}(t)) ight] dt onumber
&= \int_0^T \left[ rac{\partial H}{\partial x} \delta x - p^T \cdot \delta \dot{x} ight] dt onumber \end{align}

Proof of \eqref{eq:ii}:

From the result of \eqref{eq:i}: \(\delta \mathcal{L} = \int_0^T \left[ rac{\partial H}{\partial x} \cdot \delta x - p^T \delta \dot{x} ight] dt = 0\)

Considering the second term separately and applying integration by parts: egin{align} \int_0^T p^T (\delta \dot{x}) \, dt &= \int_0^T p^T \cdot d(\delta x) onumber
&= \left[ p^T \cdot \delta x ight]_0^T - \int_0^T \delta x \cdot d(p^T) onumber
&= p^T(T) \cdot \delta x(T) - p^T(0) \cdot \delta x(0) - \int_0^T \delta x \cdot \dot{p}^T dt onumber \end{align} Since the initial state is fixed $x(0) = x_0$, we have $\delta x(0) = 0$.

On the other hand, considering the general problem with the addition of $\Phi(x(T))$:

Taking the total variation for $\mathcal{L}$: egin{align} \delta \mathcal{L} &= \delta ig( \Phi(x(T)) ig) + \int_0^T \left( rac{\partial H}{\partial x} \delta x + \dot{p}^T \cdot \delta x ight) dt - p^T(T) \cdot \delta x(T) onumber
&= I + rac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x} \cdot \delta x - p^T(T) \cdot \delta x(T) onumber
&= I + \left[ abla \Phi(x(T))^T \cdot \delta x(T) - p^T(T) \cdot \delta x(T) ight] onumber \end{align} (where $I$ is the integral part that equates to $0$ to yield the adjoint equation). For $\delta \mathcal{L} = 0$ at the boundary, we must have: \( abla \Phi(x(T)) = p(T) \quad ext{(Transversality Condition)}\)

b. State Equation

We need to prove $\dot{x}^*(t) = rac{\partial H}{\partial p}$. According to the initial problem setup: egin{equation} \dot{x}(t) = f(x, u) \label{eq:state_pmp} \end{equation} By the definition of the Hamiltonian: $H(x, u, p) = p^T \cdot f(x, u) + L(x, u)$. Taking the derivative of $H$ with respect to $p$, we obtain: egin{equation} rac{\partial H}{\partial p} = f(x, u) \label{eq:H_deriv_p} \end{equation} From \eqref{eq:state_pmp} and \eqref{eq:H_deriv_p}, we deduce: \( rac{\partial H}{\partial p} = \dot{x}^*(t)\)

c. Control Optimization Condition

On the other hand, consider the functional: $\mathcal{L} = \int_0^T \left( H(x, u, p) - p^T \dot{x} ight) dt$. Taking the variation with respect to $u$ (equivalent to taking the derivative with respect to $u$ and multiplying by $\delta u$): \(\delta_u \mathcal{L} = \int_0^T \left( rac{\partial H}{\partial u} \cdot \delta u ight) dt\) Because $ rac{d\mathcal{L}}{du} = \int_0^T rac{\partial H}{\partial u} dt$. For optimization, we force $\delta_u \mathcal{L} = 0$ for any arbitrary variation $\delta u$. Thus, we deduce: \( rac{\partial H}{\partial u} = 0\)

2. The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equation

HJB is the continuous-time version of Bellman’s Principle of Optimality in Dynamic Programming. This principle simply states: “Whatever your current state is and however you got there, the decisions from this point forward must constitute an optimal strategy for the remainder of the journey.”

Reference: Donald E. Kirk, “Optimal Control Theory: An Introduction”, Section 3.11.

In the initial approach to dynamic programming, we approximated continuous-time systems with discrete systems. This approach leads to a recurrence relation ideal for computer solutions. In this section, we will consider an alternative approach that leads to a nonlinear partial differential equation — the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (H-J-B) equation.

Statement of the Problem

Consider the process described by the state equation: egin{equation} \dot{x}(t) = f(x(t), u(t)) \label{eq:state_HJB} \end{equation} This process needs to be controlled to minimize the performance measure (cost function): egin{equation} J = \Phi(x(T)) + \int_0^T L(x( au), u( au)) d au \label{eq:cost_HJB} \end{equation} where $\Phi$ and $L$ are given functions, the start time $0$ and terminal time $T$ are fixed, and $ au$ is a dummy integration variable.

The Partial Differential Equation (PDE) named Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman is given by: egin{equation} - rac{\partial J^}{\partial t}(x(t), t) = H(x(t), u^(x(t), abla_x J^, t), abla_x J^). \label{eq:3.11-10a_initial} \end{equation}

Proof

We use the imbedding principle to include this problem in a broader class of problems by considering the cost function from an arbitrary time $t$: egin{equation} J(x(t), t, u( au)) = \Phi(x(T)) + \int_t^T L(x( au), u( au)) d au \label{eq:imbedding} \end{equation} where $t$ can be any value less than or equal to $T$ ($t \le T$), and $x(t)$ can be any valid state value.

Let $J^(x(t), t)$ be the optimal cost to go from state $x(t)$ at time $t$ to the terminal time $T$. The optimal value function is defined as: egin{equation} J^(x(t), t) = \min_{\substack{u( au) \ t \le au \le T}} \left{ \Phi(x(T)) + \int_t^T L(x( au), u( au)) d au ight} \end{equation}

By subdividing the integration interval into two segments $[t, t+\Delta t]$ and $[t+\Delta t, T]$, we obtain: egin{equation} J^*(x(t), t) = \min_{\substack{u( au) \ t \le au \le T}} \left{ \int_t^{t+\Delta t} L(x( au), u( au)) d au + \int_{t+\Delta t}^T L(x( au), u( au)) d au + \Phi(x(T)) ight} \label{eq:subdivide} \end{equation}

According to Bellman’s Principle of Optimality, the optimal trajectory has a nested property. Therefore, we can optimize over the first small interval $\Delta t$, and the remainder is exactly the optimal cost function starting from $t+\Delta t$: egin{equation} J^(x(t), t) = \min_{\substack{u( au) \ t \le au \le t+\Delta t}} \left{ \int_t^{t+\Delta t} L(x( au), u( au)) d au + J^(x(t+\Delta t), t+\Delta t) ight} \label{eq:principle_opt} \end{equation}

(From equation \eqref{eq:principle_opt}, by expanding the Taylor series for $J^(x(t+\Delta t), t+\Delta t)$ and letting $\Delta t o 0$, we will obtain the complete HJB partial differential equation.)*

Here, $J^*(x(t + \Delta t), t + \Delta t)$ is the minimum cost of the process in the time interval $t + \Delta t \le au \le T$, with the “initial” state being $x(t + \Delta t)$.

Assuming that the second-order partial derivatives of $J^$ exist and are bounded, we can expand the Taylor series for $J^(x(t + \Delta t), t + \Delta t)$ around the point $(x(t), t)$ to obtain: egin{align} J^(x(t), t) = \min_{\substack{u( au) \ t \le au \le t+\Delta t}} \Bigg{ &\int_t^{t+\Delta t} L(x( au), u( au)) d au + J^(x(t), t) + \left[ rac{\partial J^}{\partial t}(x(t), t) ight] \Delta t onumber
&+ \left[ rac{\partial J^}{\partial x}(x(t), t) ight]^T [x(t + \Delta t) - x(t)] + ext{higher-order terms} \Bigg} \label{eq:taylor_expansion} \end{align}

Now, considering a sufficiently small $\Delta t$. We can approximate the integral and the state variation as follows:

  • $\int_t^{t+\Delta t} L(x( au), u( au)) d au \approx L(x(t), u(t)) \Delta t$
  • $x(t + \Delta t) - x(t) \approx \dot{x}(t) \Delta t = f(x(t), u(t)) \Delta t$

Substituting these approximations into equation \eqref{eq:taylor_expansion}, we obtain: egin{align} J^(x(t), t) = \min_{u(t)} \Big{ &L(x(t), u(t)) \Delta t + J^(x(t), t) + J_t^(x(t), t) \Delta t onumber
&+ J_x^{T}(x(t), t) \left[ f(x(t), u(t)) ight] \Delta t + o(\Delta t) \Big} \label{eq:small_dt} \end{align} where $J_t^* = rac{\partial J^}{\partial t}$, $J_x^ = rac{\partial J^}{\partial x} = abla_x J^$, and $o(\Delta t)$ denotes the terms containing $(\Delta t)^2$ and higher-order infinitesimals of $\Delta t$ arising from the integral approximation and Taylor series truncation.

Next, since the quantities $J^(x(t), t)$ and $J_t^(x(t), t) \Delta t$ do not depend on the control variable $u(t)$, we can move them outside the minimization operator: \(J^*(x(t), t) = J^*(x(t), t) + J_t^*(x(t), t) \Delta t + \min_{u(t)} \Big\{ L(x(t), u(t)) \Delta t + J_x^{*T}(x(t), t) f(x(t), u(t)) \Delta t + o(\Delta t) \Big\}\)

Canceling $J^(x(t), t)$ on both sides, dividing the entire equation by $\Delta t$, and moving $J_t^$ to the other side: \(-J_t^*(x(t), t) = \min_{u(t)} \left\{ L(x(t), u(t)) + J_x^{*T}(x(t), t) f(x(t), u(t)) + rac{o(\Delta t)}{\Delta t} ight\}\)

Finally, taking the limit as $\Delta t o 0$, the term $ rac{o(\Delta t)}{\Delta t}$ approaches $0$. We obtain the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) partial differential equation: egin{equation} - rac{\partial J^(x, t)}{\partial t} = \min_{u(t)} \left[ L(x, u) + abla_x J^(x, t)^T f(x, u) ight] \label{eq:hjb_final} \end{equation}

With the boundary condition at the terminal time $T$: egin{equation} J^(x(T), T) = \Phi(x(T)) \label{eq:hjb_boundary} \end{equation} From the minimization [since these quantities do not depend on $u(t)$], we obtain: egin{align} 0 &= rac{\partial J^}{\partial t}(x(t), t) \Delta t + \min_{u(t)} \Big{ L(x(t), u(t)) \Delta t onumber
&\quad + abla_x J^*(x(t), t)^T f(x(t), u(t)) \Delta t + o(\Delta t) \Big}. \label{eq:3.11-9} \end{align}

Dividing both sides by $\Delta t$ and taking the limit as $\Delta t o 0$, we have: egin{equation} 0 = rac{\partial J^}{\partial t}(x(t), t) + \min_{u(t)} \left{ L(x(t), u(t)) + abla_x J^(x(t), t)^T f(x(t), u(t)) ight}. \label{eq:3.11-10} \end{equation}

To find the boundary value for this PDE, we set $t = T$; from the definition of the initial cost function, it is clear that: egin{equation} J^*(x(T), T) = \Phi(x(T)). \label{eq:3.11-11} \end{equation}

We define the Hamiltonian function $H$ as: egin{equation} H(x(t), u(t), abla_x J^) riangleq L(x(t), u(t)) + abla_x J^(x(t), t)^T f(x(t), u(t)) \label{eq:3.11-12} \end{equation} and egin{equation} H(x(t), u^(x(t), abla_x J^, t), abla_x J^) = \min_{u(t)} H(x(t), u(t), abla_x J^), \label{eq:3.11-13} \end{equation} because the minimizing control signal will depend on $x$, $ abla_x J^$, and $t$. Using these definitions, we obtain the Hamilton-Jacobi equation: egin{equation} 0 = rac{\partial J^}{\partial t}(x(t), t) + H(x(t), u^(x(t), abla_x J^, t), abla_x J^*). \label{eq:3.11-10a} \end{equation}

This equation is the continuous-time analogue of Bellman’s recurrence equation; therefore, we will refer to equation \eqref{eq:3.11-10a} as the “Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation”.

3. A Calculus Example

Reference: Donald E. Kirk, “Optimal Control Theory: An Introduction”, Example 3.11-1.

A first-order system is described by the differential equation: egin{equation} \dot{x}(t) = f(x(t), u(t)) = x(t) + u(t); \label{eq:3.11-14} \end{equation} We need to find the optimal control law that minimizes the performance measure (cost function): egin{equation} J = \Phi(x(T)) + \int_0^T L(x(t), u(t)) dt = rac{1}{4}x^2(T) + \int_0^T rac{1}{4}u^2(t) dt. \label{eq:3.11-15} \end{equation} The terminal time $T$ is specified, and the state values as well as the control signals are not restricted by any boundary constraints.

Solve by the HJB Equation

Substituting $L(x(t), u(t)) = rac{1}{4}u^2(t)$ and $f(x(t), u(t)) = x(t) + u(t)$ into the Hamiltonian definition, we have the Hamiltonian function (for brevity, we omit the arguments of $ abla_x J^$): egin{equation} H(x(t), u(t), abla_x J^, t) = rac{1}{4}u^2(t) + abla_x J^* \cdot [x(t) + u(t)], \label{eq:3.11-16} \end{equation} and since the control signal is unconstrained, the necessary condition that the optimal control must satisfy is: egin{equation} rac{\partial H}{\partial u} = rac{1}{2}u(t) + abla_x J^*(x(t), t) = 0. \label{eq:3.11-17} \end{equation}

Observing that: egin{equation} rac{\partial^2 H}{\partial u^2} = rac{1}{2} > 0; \label{eq:3.11-18} \end{equation} therefore, the control signal satisfying equation \eqref{eq:3.11-17} truly minimizes the function $H$. From \eqref{eq:3.11-17}, we deduce: egin{equation} u^(t) = -2 abla_x J^(x(t), t), \label{eq:3.11-19} \end{equation} Substituting this $u^(t)$ value into the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation $\left(0 = rac{\partial J^}{\partial t} + H ight)$, we get: egin{align} 0 &= rac{\partial J^}{\partial t} + rac{1}{4}[-2 abla_x J^]^2 + [ abla_x J^]x(t) - 2[ abla_x J^]^2 onumber
&= rac{\partial J^}{\partial t} - [ abla_x J^]^2 + [ abla_x J^]x(t). \label{eq:3.11-20} \end{align} From \eqref{eq:3.11-15}, the boundary value is: egin{equation} J^(x(T), T) = rac{1}{4}x^2(T). \label{eq:3.11-21} \end{equation}

One way to solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation is to guess a form for the solution and verify if it satisfies the differential equation and boundary conditions. Assume the solution has the form: egin{equation} J^(x(t), t) = rac{1}{2} K(t) x^2(t), \label{eq:3.11-22} \end{equation} where $K(t)$ represents a scalar function of $t$ to be determined. Note that: egin{equation} abla_x J^(x(t), t) = K(t) x(t), \label{eq:3.11-23} \end{equation} combining with equation \eqref{eq:3.11-19}, we deduce: egin{equation} u^(t) = -2K(t)x(t). \label{eq:3.11-24} \end{equation} Thus, if we can find a function $K(t)$ satisfying \eqref{eq:3.11-20} and \eqref{eq:3.11-21}, the optimal control law will be a *linear feedback of the state — in fact, this is the motivation for choosing the assumed solution form \eqref{eq:3.11-22}.

By choosing $K(T) = rac{1}{2}$, the assumed solution will match the specified boundary condition \eqref{eq:3.11-21}. Substituting \eqref{eq:3.11-23} for $ abla_x J^*$ and substituting \( rac{\partial J^*}{\partial t}(x(t), t) = rac{1}{2} \dot{K}(t) x^2(t)\) into equation \eqref{eq:3.11-20}, we get: egin{equation} 0 = rac{1}{2} \dot{K}(t) x^2(t) - K^2(t) x^2(t) + K(t) x^2(t). \label{eq:3.11-25} \end{equation} Since this equation must be satisfied for all $x(t)$, we have: egin{equation} rac{1}{2} \dot{K}(t) - K^2(t) + K(t) = 0. \label{eq:3.11-26} \end{equation} $K(t)$ is a scalar function of $t$; therefore, the solution can be found using separation of variables, yielding: egin{equation} K(t) = rac{e^{(T-t)}}{e^{(T-t)} + e^{-(T-t)}}. \label{eq:3.11-27} \end{equation}

Then, the optimal control law is: egin{align} u^(t) &= -2 abla_x J^(x(t), t) onumber
&= -2K(t)x(t). \label{eq:3.11-28} \end{align}

Note that as $T o \infty$, this linear time-varying feedback approaches a constant feedback ($K(t) o 1$), and the controlled system: egin{align} \dot{x}(t) &= x(t) - 2x(t) onumber
&= -x(t) \label{eq:3.11-29} \end{align} becomes stable. If this did not occur, the value of the performance measure would approach infinity.

Solve by the Pontryagin’s maximum principle

egin{align} ext{System dynamics:} \quad &\dot{x}(t) = x(t) + u(t) onumber
ext{Cost function:} \quad &J = rac{1}{4}x^2(T) + \int_0^T rac{1}{4}u^2(t) dt onumber \end{align}

By definition, the Hamiltonian function for this problem is: egin{align} H(x, u, p) &= L(x, u) + p(t) f(x, u) onumber
&= rac{1}{4}u^2(t) + p(t)[x(t) + u(t)] \label{eq:pmp_H} \end{align}

According to Pontryagin’s maximum principle, the optimal trajectory must satisfy 3 equations: egin{equation} rac{\partial H}{\partial u} = 0 \implies rac{1}{2}u(t) + p(t) = 0 \implies u^*(t) = -2p(t) \label{eq:pmp_u} \end{equation} egin{equation} \dot{x}(t) = rac{\partial H}{\partial p} = x(t) + u(t) = x(t) - 2p(t) \label{eq:pmp_state} \end{equation} egin{equation} \dot{p}(t) = - rac{\partial H}{\partial x} = -p(t) \label{eq:pmp_adjoint} \end{equation} At the terminal time $T$, the dual variable $p(T)$ is determined by the derivative of the terminal cost function $\Phi(x(T)) = rac{1}{4}x^2(T)$: egin{equation} p(T) = abla_x \Phi(x(T)) = rac{1}{2}x(T) \label{eq:pmp_transversality} \end{equation}

Solving the system of equations via the Sweep Method

From \eqref{eq:pmp_state} and \eqref{eq:pmp_adjoint}, we have a Two-Point Boundary Value Problem. To find the feedback control law, we assume a linear relationship between the dual variable $p(t)$ and the state $x(t)$: egin{equation} p(t) = K(t)x(t) \label{eq:pmp_riccati_sub} \end{equation} Taking the derivative of both sides with respect to time $t$: egin{equation} \dot{p}(t) = \dot{K}(t)x(t) + K(t)\dot{x}(t) \label{eq:pmp_dp} \end{equation}

Now, we substitute $\dot{p}(t)$ from \eqref{eq:pmp_adjoint} and $\dot{x}(t)$ from \eqref{eq:pmp_state} into equation \eqref{eq:pmp_dp}: \(-p(t) = \dot{K}(t)x(t) + K(t)[x(t) - 2p(t)]\) Further substituting $p(t) = K(t)x(t)$ into both sides: \(-K(t)x(t) = \dot{K}(t)x(t) + K(t)x(t) - 2K^2(t)x(t)\) Since this relation must hold for all state trajectories $x(t) eq 0$, we can cancel $x(t)$ on both sides: \(-K(t) = \dot{K}(t) + K(t) - 2K^2(t)\) Rearranging, we obtain the Riccati differential equation for the function $K(t)$: egin{equation} rac{1}{2}\dot{K}(t) + K(t) - K^2(t) = 0 \label{eq:pmp_riccati} \end{equation}

Considering the boundary condition from equation \eqref{eq:pmp_transversality}: \(p(T) = K(T)x(T) = rac{1}{2}x(T) \implies K(T) = rac{1}{2}\)

Conclusion:

The differential equation \eqref{eq:pmp_riccati} and boundary condition $K(T) = rac{1}{2}$ yield equation \eqref{eq:3.11-26}, similar to the HJB method. Optimal control law: \(u^*(t) = -2p(t) = -2K(t)x(t)\)

Therefore, we also have the following relationship: \(p(t) = abla_x J^*(x, t) = K(t)x(t)\)
entry.summary: Notes on the mathematical foundations of Optimal Control Theory, including PMP and Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman derivations.
